notes.short: God's sorrow over sin, told in human words
notes.about: Scripture tells of the LORD's regret and grief in human words, so that we can understand His sorrow over sin. The same Bible says He “is not a man, that He should change His mind” (1 Samuel 15:29).

figure.name: Anthropopatheia
figure.means: God's sorrow over man's sin, told in human words

hebrew.note: “Regretted” is nacham, the word Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 use when they say God does not “change His mind”.

notes.evidence: Bullinger lists Genesis 6:6 under Anthropopatheia, human feelings spoken of God. Gill calls it speaking after the manner of men, Keil and Delitzsch an anthropomorphic expression, and Wesley, Barnes and Jamieson, Fausset and Brown say the same in their own words. Numbers 23:19 and 1 Samuel 15:29 hold the other side.
notes.limit: The writers agree the words are a figure, but not on how far the feeling is like ours: Keil and Delitzsch speak of the pain of the divine love at man's sin, while Gill says there can be no uneasiness in God's mind.

cites.quote: not that He has such feelings; but, in infinite condescension, He is thus spoken of in order to enable us to comprehend Him.
This is speaking by an anthropopathy, after the manner of men
The repentance of God is an anthropomorphic expression for the pain of the divine love at the sin of man
These are expressions after the manner of men, and must be understood so as not to reflect upon God's immutability or felicity.
man has a finite mind and a limited sphere of observation, and therefore is not able to conceive or express thoughts or acts exactly as they are in God, but only as they are in himself.
by language suited to our nature and experience, He is described as about to alter His visible procedure towards mankind
